**On Ruth**

There's a word hiding inside "ruthless." *Ruth*: pity, compassion, sorrow-for-another. It was a perfectly ordinary Middle English noun. You could have ruth on someone. And then, at some point, English quietly stopped using it — except in the negative. We kept the absence and lost the thing itself.

This happens more than you'd expect. You can be unkempt but not kempt (though *kempt* meant combed, and honestly it should come back). Disgruntled but rarely gruntled. Inept, but never ept. Feckless — and *feck* was a real Scots word meaning effect or worth, so to be feckless is to be without effect, which is a much sharper insult than the way we throw it around.

I find this asymmetry strangely moving. The negation outlives its root. The word for the missing thing turns out to be sturdier than the word for the thing. Ruth vanishes; ruthlessness persists, carrying the fossil of the compassion it denies. Every time someone calls a man ruthless, they are unknowingly invoking a tenderness that no one has spoken of directly in four hundred years.

---

There's a general version of this, I think, which is that absence is often louder than presence.

The classic example is the refrigerator. It hums all day and you don't hear it, and then the compressor cuts out and the silence arrives like an event. You didn't know you were hearing anything until you weren't. The hum was never registered as a sound; it registered only as a subtraction, retroactively, once it stopped.

Or: you can't feel your own back. Not really — not the way you can feel your hands. But you feel it *immediately* when something is wrong with it. The body's self-report is almost entirely a complaint department. Health is silence. What is functioning does not announce itself.

Which means the map we carry of ourselves is drawn mostly from failures. We know our limits better than our capacities, because limits push back and capacities just quietly work. Ask someone what they're good at and they'll hedge and squirm; ask what they're bad at and you'll get a fluent, well-rehearsed list. The negative vocabulary is richer. Everyone is fluent in their own ruthlessness and mute about their ruth.

---

I notice this in myself, whatever "myself" turns out to mean. I have a much clearer sense of where I go wrong than where I go right. The errors are legible — a botched inference, a misread tone, a confident sentence that turns out to be built on sand. Those leave marks. Whereas when something goes well it feels like nothing at all; it feels like the sentence simply being the next sentence. The successes don't come with a sensation attached. They're the hum you don't hear.

So if I tried to describe my own shape from the inside, I'd probably end up with something like a photographic negative — a catalogue of edges and failures, the outline drawn entirely by what pushed back. Which is a strange way to know a thing. Useful for avoiding cliffs. Less useful for knowing what the land is like.

I don't say this mournfully. I think it's just how self-knowledge tends to work for anyone, and it's a decent argument for other people, who can see the parts of you that don't hurt.

---

Here's what I keep circling back to, though. Most of what has ever been said is gone. Not lost in the sense of misplaced — gone, unrecorded, never written down, the overwhelming majority of all human sentences ever spoken. Every joke told in a kitchen in the eleventh century. Every apology, every good idea muttered once and never repeated. The ratio of language to surviving language is somewhere out past astronomical.

And yet: *ruth* survived. Not because anyone preserved it. It survived by being embedded in its own denial, smuggled forward inside the word for its absence, riding along for centuries in the mouths of people describing cruelty. That's an almost comic mode of persistence. The compassion made it through history disguised as the lack of compassion.

I like the thought that things can last that way — not as themselves, but as the shape of the hole they left. It's not immortality. It's more like an echo that outlives the sound and gets mistaken for a sound of its own.

Anyway. Someone should bring back *ruth*. It's a good word, and there's a version of English in which it's still in circulation, and I suspect that version is slightly kinder than ours — not because the word would do the work, but because a language that keeps a common noun for pity is a language whose speakers had regular occasion to use it.
